Odd
OD
a. (remaining after an even number is subtracted; extra; not matching a set)
Old Norse oddi, a point of land, a triangle, hence a third or extra thing that does not pair evenly with another. An odd number is, at root, the number left standing alone once everything else has been paired off.

Biblical Definition

Numbers' census of the Levites, taken by the month and upward rather than by the usual military age of twenty, produces a specific and awkward mismatch that the text handles with remarkable practical care. The firstborn of Israel numbered 22,273; the Levites numbered only 22,000, leaving the odd number of them — the 273 firstborn sons with no Levite substitute to redeem them by direct exchange — to be redeemed instead by a fixed payment of five shekels apiece, the money given to Aaron and his sons. The arithmetic did not come out even, and rather than round the number away or ignore the remainder, the law makes specific, individual provision for every single odd, unmatched firstborn son.

What the text quietly insists on is that an odd number, a remainder left over after the neat one-to-one substitution has been exhausted, is not a rounding error beneath the law's notice. Each of the 273 firstborn sons represented was a particular household's particular son, owed to the LORD by the same claim as every other firstborn in Israel, and the text will not let the census close until every one of them, down to the last odd man, has been accounted for and redeemed by name-equivalent payment. The God who counts a whole nation by tribe and family is shown, in this one administrative detail, also counting the leftover fraction that a less careful record might have simply dropped.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): not even; not exactly divisible by two; also, remaining over and above a certain number.

expand to see more

ODD, a. Not even; that cannot be divided into two equal whole numbers; also, additional, over and above a stated round number.

REDEEM, v.t. To buy back; to ransom; to release from obligation or bondage by payment.

FIRSTBORN, n. The first offspring, especially of a family, holding a place of preeminence and, under the law, dedicated to the LORD.

SHEKEL, n. A Hebrew unit of weight and, later, of currency, used as the standard of the sanctuary.

SUBSTITUTE, n. One put in place of another; something used instead of another thing.

Key Scripture

Num 3:46 — "And for those that are to be redeemed of the two hundred and threescore and thirteen of the firstborn of the children of Israel, which are more than the Levites;"

Num 3:47 — "Thou shalt even take five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary shalt thou take them: (the shekel is twenty gerahs:)"

Num 3:48 — "And thou shalt give the money, wherewith the odd number of them is to be redeemed, unto Aaron and to his sons."

Num 3:12 — "And I, behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine;"

Modern Corruption

A leftover remainder is treated as beneath careful accounting, a rounding error to be waved past, when Numbers three insists on redeeming every single odd, unmatched firstborn son by name-equivalent payment rather than letting the surplus simply go unaddressed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; odd still names what is left over after an even division. The principle worth recovering is the law's evident refusal to treat 273 individual firstborn sons as a statistical remainder rather than as 273 actual persons, each with a genuine claim on redemption that a tidier, rounder number would have satisfied automatically through the Levite substitution.

The five-shekel payment is not a discount or an approximation; it is a precise, individually calculated redemption price applied to precisely the number of people the neat substitution could not cover. A God who orders the substitution of an entire tribe for an entire category of firstborn sons, and then pauses to make sure the 273 who fall outside that clean exchange are not simply absorbed into the total, is shown counting in a way that leaves no odd remainder actually unaccounted for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew adaph (H5736), to be over and above, to remain in excess; the verb behind “the odd number” in Numbers 3:48, describing an exact numerical surplus.

expand to see more

Hebrew adaph (H5736) — to be over, to remain in excess, to be a surplus; the root behind “the odd number of them” in Numbers 3:48.

Hebrew padah (H6299) — to redeem, to ransom, to buy back; the standing verb for the whole transaction this passage describes.

Hebrew bekor (H1060) — a firstborn; the category of person whose redemption the odd number concerns.

Hebrew sheqel (H8255) — a shekel, a unit of weight and money; the standard of payment fixed for each odd, unmatched firstborn.

Hebrew tachath (H8478) — instead of, in the place of; the preposition governing the whole logic of Levite-for-firstborn substitution in Numbers 3:12.

Usage

"“the odd number of them is to be redeemed” — the precise, individually accounted surplus of firstborn sons."

"“five shekels apiece by the poll” — the fixed redemption price for each one."

"“the Levites shall be mine” — the substitution the odd number fell outside of, and so required its own provision."
